records.source: וַ֭יַּעַן צֹפַ֥ר הַנַּֽעֲמָתִ֗י וַיֹּאמַֽר׃
records.gloss: And answered Zophar the Naamathite and said:
pieces: Then Zophar the Naamathite answered:

L.1: And Zophar the Naamathite answered and said:

decisions.choice: Zophar the Naamathite: the third of Job's friends
decisions.reason: Zophar was introduced in 2:11 and first spoke in chapter 11. This is his second speech and, as the text stands, his last: he has no third speech after chapter 26. "Naamathite" names his people or home, which is not known for certain.

decisions.choice: answered and said: the usual opening of a speech
decisions.reason: "He answered and said" introduces each speech in the dialogue (4:1; 8:1; 11:1). Zophar answers Job's speech in chapter 19.
Balanced and Readable use one English verb for the Hebrew pair, the book's pattern for speech introductions. The introduction stays prose.

records.heading: The joy of the godless lasts only a moment

records.source: לָ֭כֵן שְׂעִפַּ֣י יְשִׁיב֑וּנִי וּ֝בַעֲב֗וּר ח֣וּשִׁי בִֽי׃
records.gloss: Therefore my disquieting thoughts make me answer, and because of my agitation in me.
pieces: So my troubled thoughts urge me to reply, \q because I am deeply stirred.

L.2: Therefore my troubled thoughts make me answer, \q because of the agitation within me.

R.2: My troubled thoughts make me answer you, \q because I am so upset inside.

decisions.reason: The word (se'ippim) means thoughts that trouble and divide the mind. Eliphaz used it of the night thoughts in which a vision came to him (4:13).

decisions.choice: my agitation: the inner stir that hurries him to speak
decisions.reason: The verb (chush) means to hurry or to be stirred up. Zophar feels pressed to answer at once.

decisions.choice: therefore: a reply to Job's last words
decisions.reason: "Therefore" ties Zophar's reply to what Job has just said, above all his warning that the friends themselves should fear the sword of judgment (19:28-29).

decisions.choice: So ... deeply stirred / so upset inside
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the abstract noun into a plain clause about how Zophar feels.

records.source: מוּסַ֣ר כְּלִמָּתִ֣י אֶשְׁמָ֑ע וְ֝ר֗וּחַ מִֽבִּינָתִ֥י יַעֲנֵֽנִי׃
records.gloss: [The] correction of my insult I hear, and a spirit from my understanding answers me.
pieces: I have heard a rebuke that insults me, \q and out of my understanding my spirit gives me a reply.

L.3: I hear a rebuke that insults me, \q and a spirit from my understanding answers me.

R.3: I have heard you scold me, and it insults me. \q But my spirit understands and tells me what to answer.

decisions.choice: a rebuke that insults me: a correction that shames me
decisions.reason: Musar is correction or discipline; kelimmah is disgrace. Zophar takes Job's words in 19:2-6 and 19:28-29 as a rebuke that puts him to shame.

decisions.choice: a spirit from my understanding: Zophar's own inner spirit, prompted by what he understands
alternatives: a spirit beyond my understanding answers me
decisions.reason: Ruach here is the human spirit, the inner self that moves a person to speak (32:18). The preposition "from" can also mean "beyond", which would make it an outside spirit inspiring him, as Eliphaz claimed a spirit spoke to him (4:15); "from my understanding" fits the parallel with his own thoughts in verse 2.
Balanced and Readable say "my spirit" to make clear it is Zophar's own (m2).

records.source: הֲזֹ֣את יָ֭דַעְתָּ מִנִּי־עַ֑ד מִנִּ֤י שִׂ֖ים אָדָ֣ם עֲלֵי־אָֽרֶץ׃
records.gloss: Do you know this from antiquity, from [when one] placed humankind on earth,
pieces: Surely you know how it has been from of old, \q ever since humans were placed on the earth,

L.4: Do you know this from of old, \q since humankind was placed on [the] earth,

R.4: Surely you know what has been true since long ago, \q ever since God put people on the earth:

decisions.choice: Do you know this?: a question that expects "yes"
decisions.reason: Zophar does not doubt that Job knows it. The question means "Surely you know": this is what everyone has always known (compare 8:8-10; 15:18). The sentence runs on into verse 5, which says what "this" is.

decisions.choice: since humankind was placed on earth: since the creation of human beings
decisions.reason: The phrase reaches back to the beginning (Deuteronomy 4:32; Genesis 2:7). The verb has no stated subject; it is God who placed human beings on the earth.
Balanced and Readable turn the question into the statement it means (m1).
Readable names God as the one who placed people on the earth, which the Hebrew implies (m2).

records.source: כִּ֤י רִנְנַ֣ת רְ֭שָׁעִים מִקָּר֑וֹב וְשִׂמְחַ֖ת חָנֵ֣ף עֲדֵי־רָֽגַע׃
records.gloss: that the shout of joy of [the] wicked [is] from near, and the gladness of [the] godless until a moment?
pieces: that the triumph of the wicked is brief, \q and the joy of the godless lasts only a moment.

L.5: that the rejoicing of [the] wicked [is] short, \q and the joy of the godless [lasts] for a moment?

R.5: Wicked people do not shout for joy for long; \q the happiness of the godless lasts only a moment.

decisions.reason: "From near" means close at hand in time, so soon over. The second line says the same: the joy lasts "until a moment".

decisions.choice: the godless: those who turn from God
decisions.reason: The word (chanef) is used in Job for the person who has turned from God, whatever he seems to be (8:13; 13:16; 15:34). Zophar's whole speech describes what happens to such a person.

decisions.choice: rejoicing: a shout of joy or triumph
decisions.reason: Renanah is a ringing cry of joy (3:7). It is the loud triumph of the wicked when things go well for them.

records.source: אִם־יַעֲלֶ֣ה לַשָּׁמַ֣יִם שִׂיא֑וֹ וְ֝רֹאשׁ֗וֹ לָעָ֥ב יַגִּֽיעַ׃
records.gloss: Though goes up to the heavens his height, and his head to [the] cloud[s] reaches,
pieces: Though their pride rises up to the heavens \q and their heads touch the clouds,

L.6: Though his height goes up to the heavens \q and his head reaches to the clouds,

R.6: Even if wicked people rise as high as the sky \q and their heads touch the clouds,

decisions.choice: his height: his loftiness, with the sense of pride
decisions.reason: The word (si') occurs only here. It comes from the verb "to rise" and means height or exaltation; in a wicked person it is pride.

decisions.choice: up to the heavens: the proud who try to reach heaven
decisions.reason: The picture recalls the tower of Babel, whose builders wanted its top in the heavens (Genesis 11:4), and the king who said he would climb above the clouds (Isaiah 14:13-14).

decisions.choice: though: the sentence runs on into verse 7
decisions.reason: "Though" begins a condition whose result comes in verse 7: however high he rises, he will perish.
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).
Readable names who is meant, since a new reader would not know whose height is meant.

records.source: כְּֽ֭גֶלֲלוֹ לָנֶ֣צַח יֹאבֵ֑ד רֹ֝אָ֗יו יֹאמְר֥וּ אַיּֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: Like his dung forever he will perish; those who saw him will say, Where [is] he?
pieces: they will perish forever like their own dung; \q those who used to see them will ask, "Where are they?"

L.7: like his own dung he will perish forever; \q those who saw him will say, "Where [is] he?"

R.7: they will be gone forever, thrown away like dung. \q People who used to see them will ask, "Where did they go?"

decisions.choice: dung: a crude picture of contempt
decisions.reason: Gelel is dung. Zophar chooses a coarse picture on purpose: the one who rose to the clouds ends like refuse that is thrown out and gone (1 Kings 14:10 uses a related word for sweeping away filth).

decisions.choice: Where is he?: he has vanished without a trace
decisions.reason: The question means he is nowhere to be found, as Job himself said of a person who dies (14:10).
La-netsach means for all time: there is no coming back.
Readable says what the comparison means (m1).
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).

records.source: כַּחֲל֣וֹם יָ֭עוּף וְלֹ֣א יִמְצָא֑וּהוּ וְ֝יֻדַּ֗ד כְּחֶזְי֥וֹן לָֽיְלָה׃
records.gloss: Like a dream he will fly away and they will not find him, and he will be chased away like a vision of [the] night.
pieces: They will fly away like a dream and not be found; \q they will be driven off like a vision in the night.

L.8: Like a dream he will fly away, and they will not find him; \q he will be chased away like a vision of the night.

R.8: They will vanish like a dream, and no one will find them. \q They will disappear like something seen in the night.

decisions.choice: a vision of the night: a dream
decisions.reason: Chizzayon is a vision; a vision of the night is a dream (4:13; 33:15). Both lines say the same: he passes like a dream that is gone when one wakes (Psalm 73:20; Isaiah 29:7-8).

decisions.choice: they will not find him: no one will find him
decisions.reason: The plural verb has no stated subject; it means simply that he cannot be found.
The verb (nadad) means to flee or be put to flight. Bildad used it of the wicked being chased out of the world (18:18).
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).

records.source: עַ֣יִן שְׁ֭זָפַתּוּ וְלֹ֣א תוֹסִ֑יף וְלֹא־ע֝֗וֹד תְּשׁוּרֶ֥נּוּ מְקוֹמֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: An eye caught sight of him and will not again, and not again will his place behold him.
pieces: The eye that once saw them will not see them again; \q their place will look on them no more.

L.9: The eye that saw him will not [see him] again, \q and his place will no longer behold him.

R.9: People who once saw them will never see them again. \q Their own home will never see them again.

decisions.choice: the eye ... his place: Job's own words turned against him
decisions.reason: Job said of himself, "The eye of the one who sees me will not see me again," and of any who die, "his place will not know him any more" (7:8, 10). Zophar applies these words to the wicked.

decisions.choice: caught sight of: glanced at, saw
decisions.reason: The verb (shazaf) is a rare word for seeing, used of the sun that has looked on someone (Song of Songs 1:6) and of a bird's eye (28:7).
The Hebrew says only "will not again"; Literal brackets the verb English needs.
Readable says "home" for the place where the person lived.
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).

records.source: בָּ֭נָיו יְרַצּ֣וּ דַלִּ֑ים וְ֝יָדָ֗יו תָּשֵׁ֥בְנָה אוֹנֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: His sons will seek the favor of [the] poor, and his hands will give back his wealth.
pieces: Their children will have to make amends to the poor; \q their own hands must give back their wealth.

L.10: His sons will seek the favor of [the] poor, \q and his hands will give back his wealth.

R.10: Their children will have to pay back the poor, \q and they themselves will have to give back their wealth.

decisions.choice: seek the favor of the poor: have to win over and repay those he wronged
alternatives: the poor will crush his children
decisions.reason: The verb (ratsah) means to be pleased with, and in this form to seek favor or make amends (Leviticus 26:41, 43 uses it for paying off a debt of guilt). The sons must humble themselves before the poor their father robbed (20:19). A small change of one letter gives "the poor will crush his sons".
'On can mean strength (18:7, 12) or wealth (Hosea 12:9). Here, with "give back", it is the wealth he gained by force.
The word is "sons" (banim), and the plural can include daughters (8:4).
Balanced and Readable say "children" (m3); Literal keeps "sons".
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).

records.source: עַ֭צְמוֹתָיו מָלְא֣וּ עֲלוּמָ֑יו וְ֝עִמּ֗וֹ עַל־עָפָ֥ר תִּשְׁכָּֽב׃
records.gloss: His bones were full of his youthful vigor, and with him on the dust it will lie down.
pieces: Their bones were full of youthful strength, \q but it will lie down with them in the dust.

L.11: His bones were full of his youthful vigor, \q but it will lie down with him in the dust.

R.11: Their bodies were full of the strength of youth, \q but that strength will be buried with them.

decisions.choice: youthful vigor: the strength of youth
decisions.reason: 'Alumim is youth (33:25; Psalm 89:46). The word could also be taken from the verb "to hide" ('alam), giving "his secret sins", but the parallel with full bones points to youthful strength.

decisions.choice: lie down in the dust: die and be buried
decisions.reason: To lie in the dust is to be in the grave (7:21; 21:26). He dies while still strong, and his strength is buried with him.
The verb is feminine singular. It most likely refers to his vigor, though it may take the bones together as one.

alternatives: bones ... lie down with them in the dust
decisions.reason: Readable says "bodies" for the bones, which stand for the whole person, and explains the idiom (m2).
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).

records.source: אִם־תַּמְתִּ֣יק בְּפִ֣יו רָעָ֑ה יַ֝כְחִידֶ֗נָּה תַּ֣חַת לְשׁוֹנֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: Though evil tastes sweet in his mouth, he hides it under his tongue,
pieces: Though evil tastes sweet in their mouth \q and they hide it under their tongue,

L.12: Though evil is sweet in his mouth, \q [though] he hides it under his tongue,

R.12: Evil may taste sweet to the wicked, \q so that they hold it under their tongue to enjoy it longer,

decisions.choice: sweet in the mouth, hidden under the tongue: evil savored like a treat
decisions.reason: Wrongdoing is pictured as tasty food that a person holds in the mouth to make the taste last (Proverbs 9:17; 20:17).

decisions.choice: though: verses 12-13 lead up to verse 14
decisions.reason: The "though" clause runs through verse 13; the result comes in verse 14, where the sweet food turns to poison.
Readable says why someone would hold food under the tongue (m1).
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).

records.source: יַחְמֹ֣ל עָ֭לֶיהָ וְלֹ֣א יַֽעַזְבֶ֑נָּה וְ֝יִמְנָעֶ֗נָּה בְּת֣וֹךְ חִכּֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: he spares it and does not let it go, and holds it back in the midst of his palate,
pieces: though they cannot bear to let it go \q but keep it in their mouth,

L.13: [though] he spares it and does not let it go, \q and holds it back in the middle of his palate,

R.13: They cannot bear to let it go, \q so they keep it in their mouth.

decisions.choice: spares it: is loath to part with it
decisions.reason: The verb (chamal) means to have pity on or spare. He cannot bring himself to part with the sweet morsel of evil.

decisions.choice: palate: the roof of the mouth
decisions.reason: Chekh is the palate, where taste is felt (6:30; 12:11).

decisions.choice: cannot bear to let it go ... mouth
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put "spares it" into plain English and say "mouth" for the palate.
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).

records.source: לַ֭חְמוֹ בְּמֵעָ֣יו נֶהְפָּ֑ךְ מְרוֹרַ֖ת פְּתָנִ֣ים בְּקִרְבּֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: His food in his bowels is turned; [the] venom of cobras [is] in his inner parts.
pieces: their food turns sour in their stomach; \q it becomes the venom of cobras inside them.

L.14: his food in his bowels is turned; \q [it is] the venom of cobras within him.

R.14: But that food turns sour in their stomach. \q It becomes like snake poison inside them.

decisions.reason: Merorah is bitterness: the bitter gall of the body (16:13) and the venom of snakes (Deuteronomy 32:33 has a related word). The sweet food of verse 12 becomes poison.
Peten is a poisonous snake, most likely the cobra (Deuteronomy 32:33; Psalm 58:5; Isaiah 11:8).

decisions.choice: is turned: the result of verses 12-13
decisions.reason: This is the main clause the "though" of verse 12 was leading to.
Balanced and Readable say what the food is turned into.
Readable makes the comparison explicit and uses a common word for the snake.
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).

records.source: חַ֣יִל בָּ֭לַע וַיְקִאֶ֑נּוּ מִ֝בִּטְנ֗וֹ יוֹרִשֶׁ֥נּוּ אֵֽל׃
records.gloss: Wealth he swallowed, and he vomits it up; from his belly God drives it out.
pieces: They swallow riches but vomit them up again; \q God makes their stomach throw them out.

L.15: He swallowed wealth and vomits it up; \q God drives it out of his belly.

R.15: They gobble up riches, but they will vomit them up again. \q God will force those riches out of their stomach.

decisions.choice: swallowed wealth: got rich by devouring what belonged to others
decisions.reason: Swallowing is greedy taking (Proverbs 1:12). Zophar carries on the picture of food from verses 12-14: wealth seized from the poor (20:19) will not stay down.
Chayil can mean strength or wealth; with "swallow" and "vomit" it is the riches he gained (20:18).

decisions.choice: God drives it out: the first mention of God in the speech
decisions.reason: Up to here the wicked seem to fall of themselves. Now Zophar names God ('El) as the one who makes him give up what he took. The verb (yarash, in this form) means to drive out or dispossess.

decisions.choice: makes their stomach throw them out / force those riches out
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable keep the picture of vomiting from the first line, which "drives it out" continues.
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).

records.source: רֹאשׁ־פְּתָנִ֥ים יִינָ֑ק תַּֽ֝הַרְגֵ֗הוּ לְשׁ֣וֹן אֶפְעֶֽה׃
records.gloss: [The] poison of cobras he sucks; the tongue of a viper will kill him.
pieces: They suck the poison of cobras; \q the viper's fangs will kill them.

L.16: He sucks the poison of cobras; \q the tongue of a viper will kill him.

R.16: What they swallowed will be like snake poison to them, \q and it will kill them like a viper's bite.

decisions.reason: Rosh usually means "head", but a second word with the same letters means poison (Deuteronomy 32:32-33).

decisions.choice: the tongue of a viper: its deadly strike
decisions.reason: The snake's tongue stands for its strike. The poison he sucked in with his ill-gotten food (20:14) is what kills him.
'Ef'eh is a poisonous snake of the desert (Isaiah 30:6; 59:5).
Balanced says "fangs", since English readers think of a snake killing by its bite (m2).

decisions.choice: What they swallowed will be like snake poison
alternatives: they suck the poison of cobras
decisions.reason: Readable shows that the poison is the stolen wealth of verses 14-15.
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).

records.source: אַל־יֵ֥רֶא בִפְלַגּ֑וֹת נַהֲרֵ֥י נַ֝חֲלֵ֗י דְּבַ֣שׁ וְחֶמְאָֽה׃
records.gloss: Let him not look on streams, rivers, torrents of honey and curds.
pieces: They will never enjoy the streams, \q the rivers flowing with honey and cream.

L.17: He will not look on [the] streams, \q [the] rivers, [the] torrents of honey and curds.

R.17: They will never enjoy the good things of the land, \q its rivers of honey and cream.

decisions.choice: will not look on: a strong denial
decisions.reason: The negative 'al with this verb form usually expresses a wish ("let him not"), but in poetry it can state firmly what will not happen. Either way he will not enjoy them.
To look on good things is to enjoy them (Psalm 27:13; Ecclesiastes 2:1).

decisions.choice: honey and curds: the plenty of a good land
decisions.reason: Honey and milk are the riches of the land God promised (Exodus 3:8). Curds (chem'ah) are thickened milk or butter (Genesis 18:8); Job uses the word of his own past plenty (29:6).
Balanced and Readable say "cream", a rich milk food familiar to English readers; Literal keeps "curds".

decisions.choice: the good things of the land
decisions.reason: Readable says what the streams of honey and cream stand for (m3).
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).

records.source: מֵשִׁ֣יב יָ֭גָע וְלֹ֣א יִבְלָ֑ע כְּחֵ֥יל תְּ֝מוּרָת֗וֹ וְלֹ֣א יַעֲלֹֽס׃
records.gloss: Restoring [the] gain [of toil], and he does not swallow [it]; according to the wealth of his exchange, and he does not rejoice.
pieces: They must give back what they toiled for and cannot swallow it; \q they get no joy from the profits of their trading.

L.18: [He] gives back [the] fruit of [his] toil and does not swallow [it]; \q from the wealth of his trading he does not rejoice.

R.18: They will have to give back what they worked for before they can enjoy it. \q They will get no pleasure from the money they made.

decisions.choice: fruit of toil: what he gained by labor
decisions.reason: Yaga' occurs only here; it comes from the verb "to toil" and means what toil has earned.

decisions.choice: the wealth of his trading: the profit of his business
alternatives: as great as his wealth, so great the restitution he must make
decisions.reason: Temurah is exchange or trade (28:17; Ruth 4:7). The line most likely means he will not enjoy the profit he made. It can also be read as "according to the wealth of his exchange": he must give back as much as he gained.

decisions.choice: give back ... not swallow: verses 10 and 15 again
decisions.reason: "Give back" repeats verse 10 and "swallow" verse 15: what he took he must return before he can enjoy it.
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).

records.source: כִּֽי־רִ֭צַּץ עָזַ֣ב דַּלִּ֑ים בַּ֥יִת גָּ֝זַ֗ל וְלֹ֣א יִבֶנֵֽהוּ׃
records.gloss: For he crushed, he abandoned [the] poor; a house he seized and he will not build it.
pieces: For they crushed the poor and left them destitute; \q they seized houses they had not built.

L.19: For he crushed [and] abandoned [the] poor; \q he seized a house that he did not build.

R.19: This is because they crushed poor people and left them with nothing. \q They took houses that they had not built.

decisions.choice: for: the reason for his downfall
decisions.reason: "For" gives the reason for verses 15-18: he must give back what he took because he took it from the poor.

decisions.choice: crushed and abandoned: oppressed and left helpless
decisions.reason: Ritstsets is to crush or oppress (Amos 4:1; 1 Samuel 12:3-4); 'azav is to forsake. He ground down the poor and then left them to their fate.

alternatives: and he will not get to build it up
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "and he will not build it". It most likely means a house built by others, which he simply took (compare Deuteronomy 6:10-11). It may also mean that he will not live to rebuild or enjoy the house he seized.
Readable makes the link to the verses before plain (m1).
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).

records.source: כִּ֤י׀לֹא־יָדַ֣ע שָׁלֵ֣ו בְּבִטְנ֑וֹ בַּ֝חֲמוּד֗וֹ לֹ֣א יְמַלֵּֽט׃
records.gloss: For he did not know ease in his belly; with his desired [things] he will not escape.
pieces: Because their greed was never satisfied, \q they will not save any of the things they prized.

L.20: For he knew no quiet in his belly; \q with what he desired he will not escape.

R.20: Their stomach was never satisfied; they always wanted more. \q So they will not be able to keep any of the things they loved.

decisions.choice: knew no quiet in his belly: his greed never rested
decisions.reason: The belly is the seat of appetite. Shalev means at ease or quiet. His craving was never at rest.

decisions.choice: he will not save anything he treasured
alternatives: his greed let nothing escape it
decisions.reason: The verb (millet) means to let escape or to save. The line most likely means that none of his treasures will save him or be saved. It may also look back to the first line: in his greed he let nothing escape him.
Balanced says what the belly stands for (m1); Literal and Readable keep the picture.
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).

records.source: אֵין־שָׂרִ֥יד לְאָכְל֑וֹ עַל־כֵּ֝֗ן לֹא־יָחִ֥יל טוּבֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: There [is] no survivor to his eating; therefore his prosperity will not endure.
pieces: Nothing was left after they had eaten; \q therefore their prosperity will not last.

L.21: Nothing escaped his devouring; \q therefore his prosperity will not last.

R.21: They devoured everything and left nothing for anyone else. \q That is why their good times will not last.

decisions.choice: survivor: what is left, a remnant
decisions.reason: Sarid is a survivor, someone or something left (18:19). His greed left nothing behind.

decisions.choice: therefore: the punishment fits the wrong
decisions.reason: Because he devoured everything, his own good fortune will be devoured. The same word sarid comes back in 20:26: nothing will be left of him either.
Tuv is goodness, here good fortune and wealth (21:16).
Readable says plainly what the picture means (m1).
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).

records.source: בִּמְלֹ֣אות שִׂ֭פְקוֹ יֵ֣צֶר ל֑וֹ כָּל־יַ֖ד עָמֵ֣ל תְּבוֹאֶֽנּוּ׃
records.gloss: In the fullness of his plenty it will be distress to him; every hand of a sufferer will come on him.
pieces: At the height of their plenty, distress will overtake them; \q every hand of the wretched will turn against them.

L.22: In the fullness of his plenty, distress will come to him; \q every hand of [the] wretched will come against him.

R.22: Just when they have more than enough, trouble will catch them, \q and all the people they made miserable will attack them.

decisions.reason: Sefeq occurs only here and means sufficiency or abundance.
The verb (tsarar) means to be narrow or in straits. Even with plenty he will be trapped.

decisions.choice: every hand of the wretched: the people he made to suffer will strike back
alternatives: the full force of misery will come on him
decisions.reason: 'Amel, as the text is pointed, is a person who suffers; their hands turn against him. With a different vowel it is "trouble", and the line would mean that every blow of trouble comes on him.
Readable links the sufferers with the poor of verse 19, which the reading in m3 implies.
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).

records.source: יְהִ֤י׀לְמַלֵּ֬א בִטְנ֗וֹ יְֽשַׁלַּח־בּ֭וֹחֲר֣וֹן אַפּ֑וֹ וְיַמְטֵ֥ר עָ֝לֵ֗ימוֹ בִּלְחוּמֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: Let it be: to fill his belly, he will send on him the burning of his anger, and he will rain on him in his flesh.
pieces: When they are about to fill their stomach, \q God will send {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} burning anger against them \q and rain it down on them as their food.

L.23: When he is about to fill his belly, \q [God] will send the burning of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger on him \q and will rain [it] on him as his food.

R.23: Just when they are about to fill their stomach, \q God will send {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} burning anger against them, \q raining it down on them like food.

decisions.choice: let it be, to fill his belly: just when he is about to eat his fill
decisions.reason: "Let it be" with "to fill" sets the time: at the very moment he is about to fill himself.

decisions.choice: God is the one who sends: his anger
decisions.reason: The verb has no named subject, but "his anger" can only be God's, whom Zophar named in verse 15 and names again in verse 29.
Lechum may be food (from the word for bread) or flesh (Zephaniah 1:17). As food, God's anger is the meal he gets instead of the one he wanted; as flesh, it falls on his body.

decisions.choice: rain on him: anger rained down like food from heaven
decisions.reason: God rained fire on Sodom (Genesis 19:24) and rained food on Israel in the desert; when they craved more, "while the food was still in their mouths, the anger of God rose against them" (Psalm 78:24-31).
Literal brackets the subject so that "he" is not taken for the wicked person (m2).
Balanced and Readable name God (m2).
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).

records.source: יִ֭בְרַח מִנֵּ֣שֶׁק בַּרְזֶ֑ל תַּ֝חְלְפֵ֗הוּ קֶ֣שֶׁת נְחוּשָֽׁה׃
records.gloss: He will flee from a weapon of iron; a bow of bronze will pierce him.
pieces: They may run from an iron weapon, \q but an arrow from a bronze bow will pierce them.

L.24: He flees from a weapon of iron; \q a bow of bronze pierces him.

R.24: They may run away from an iron weapon, \q but an arrow from a bronze bow will hit them.

decisions.choice: escaping one danger only to meet another
decisions.reason: He gets away from one weapon and is struck by another, a picture of a doom that cannot be escaped (Amos 5:19; Isaiah 24:18).

decisions.choice: a bow of bronze: an arrow shot from a strong bow
decisions.reason: The bow stands for its arrow. A bow of bronze is a bow fitted with bronze, the strongest kind (2 Samuel 22:35; Psalm 18:35).

decisions.choice: an arrow from a bronze bow
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "arrow", since it is the arrow that pierces (m2).
Balanced and Readable show the contrast between the two lines (m1).
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).

records.source: שָׁלַף֮ וַיֵּצֵ֪א מִגֵּ֫וָ֥ה וּ֭בָרָק מִֽמְּרֹרָת֥וֹ יַהֲלֹ֗ךְ עָלָ֥יו אֵמִֽים׃
records.gloss: He draws [it] out, and it comes out from [the] back, and lightning from his gall goes; on him [are] terrors.
pieces: It is pulled out and comes out of their back, \q the gleaming point out of their gall; \q terrors come over them.

L.25: He draws [it] out, and it comes out of [his] back, \q and the gleaming [point] out of his gall; \q terrors [are] upon him.

R.25: The arrow is pulled out through their back; \q its shining tip comes out of their body. \q Terror takes hold of them.

decisions.choice: lightning: the flashing point of the arrow
decisions.reason: Baraq is lightning; here it is the gleaming tip of the weapon (Deuteronomy 32:41; Nahum 3:3).

decisions.choice: gall: the gall bladder, the seat of a deadly wound
decisions.reason: Merorah, the word used for venom in verse 14, is here the gall in the body, as in 16:13, where Job says God spilled his gall on the ground.

decisions.choice: he draws it out: someone draws the arrow out
decisions.reason: The verb has no named subject. Either the wounded man or another pulls out the arrow; the point is that it has gone right through him.
'Emim are terrors. Bildad spoke of the terrors that chase the wicked and the king of terrors, death (18:11, 14).

decisions.choice: It is pulled out / The arrow is pulled out
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the passive, since who draws it out does not matter (m3).
Readable says "body" so the reader is not stopped by the name of an organ.
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).

records.source: כָּל־חֹשֶׁךְ֮ טָמ֪וּן לִצְפּ֫וּנָ֥יו תְּ֭אָכְלֵהוּ אֵ֣שׁ לֹֽא־נֻפָּ֑ח יֵ֖רַע שָׂרִ֣יד בְּאָהֳלֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: All darkness [is] hidden for his treasured [things]; a fire not blown will consume him; it will go badly [for] a survivor in his tent.
pieces: Total darkness is stored up for their treasures. \q A fire no one fanned will consume them, \q and anyone left in their tent will come to harm.

L.26: All darkness [is] stored up for his treasures; \q a fire not fanned will consume him; \q it will go badly [for] the survivor in his tent.

R.26: Darkness is waiting for everything they stored up. \q A fire that no human lit will burn them up, \q and anyone left in their home will suffer.

decisions.choice: darkness stored up for his treasures: disaster kept in store instead of riches
decisions.reason: "Hidden" (tamun) and "treasures" (tsefunim, things hidden away) are a play on words: what is kept in store for his hoard is darkness, that is, ruin.

decisions.choice: a fire not fanned: a fire no human hand lit
decisions.reason: A fire that no one blew on is a fire from God, like "the fire of God" that fell on Job's flocks (1:16).

decisions.choice: it will go badly for the survivor
alternatives: it will consume what is left in his tent
decisions.reason: The verb is taken here from ra'a', "to be bad": whoever is left in his tent will fare badly. With different vowels it is ra'ah, "to graze": the fire will eat up what is left. Both say nothing of his will remain.
Readable says what the picture means (m2).
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).

records.source: יְגַלּ֣וּ שָׁמַ֣יִם עֲוֺנ֑וֹ וְ֝אֶ֗רֶץ מִתְקוֹמָ֘מָ֥ה לֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: [The] heavens will reveal his iniquity, and [the] earth [will] rise up against him.
pieces: The heavens will expose their guilt, \q and the earth will rise up against them.

L.27: [The] heavens will reveal his iniquity, \q and [the] earth will rise up against him.

R.27: Heaven will show everyone the wrong they have done, \q and the earth will stand up to accuse them.

decisions.reason: Heaven and earth are called as witnesses in court (Deuteronomy 32:1; Isaiah 1:2). Job had cried, "Earth, do not cover my blood", and said his witness was in heaven (16:18-19). Zophar turns this round: heaven and earth will testify against the wicked.
'Avon is wrongdoing and the guilt it brings (7:21; 10:6).
Readable makes the court picture plain (m1).
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).

records.source: יִ֭גֶל יְב֣וּל בֵּית֑וֹ נִ֝גָּר֗וֹת בְּי֣וֹם אַפּֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: The produce of his house will go away, flowing away on the day of his anger.
pieces: The wealth of their house will be carried away, \q swept off like floodwaters on the day of God's anger.

L.28: The produce of his house will be carried off, \q flowing away on the day of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger.

R.28: Everything in their house will be carried away, \q swept off like a flood on the day God shows {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger.

decisions.choice: the produce of his house will be carried off
alternatives: a flood will carry off his house
decisions.reason: Yevul is produce or harvest, here all that his house holds. The verb (galah) means to go away or into exile. A related word, yuval, means a stream (Jeremiah 17:8); read that way, the line says a flood will carry off his house. The sense is close.

decisions.choice: flowing away: poured out like water
decisions.reason: The word (niggarot) is used of water spilled on the ground that cannot be gathered up again (2 Samuel 14:14).
The anger is God's, as in verse 23.

decisions.choice: God's anger / the day God shows his anger
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name God (m3), since "his" in this speech usually means the wicked person.
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14).

records.source: זֶ֤ה׀חֵֽלֶק־אָדָ֣ם רָ֭שָׁע מֵאֱלֹהִ֑ים וְנַחֲלַ֖ת אִמְר֣וֹ מֵאֵֽל׃פ
records.gloss: This [is] the portion of a wicked person from God, and the inheritance of his word from God.
pieces: This is what God gives to the wicked, \q the heritage God has appointed for them.

L.29: This [is] the portion of a wicked {{gender:person|man}} from God, \q and the heritage decreed for him by God.

R.29: This is what God has in store for wicked people. \q This is what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has decided they will receive.

decisions.choice: portion and heritage: what one is allotted
decisions.reason: Cheleq (portion) and nachalah (inheritance) are words for a share of land (Numbers 18:20; Joshua 19:9). Zophar uses them with grim irony: the wicked person's inheritance from God is ruin. Bildad ends his speech the same way (18:21), and Job uses nearly the same words in 27:13.

decisions.choice: his word: the decree concerning him
decisions.reason: 'Emer is a word or saying. "The heritage of his word" most likely means the share decreed for him; it may also mean the share given by God's word. The sense is the same.
Both lines name God, with two words ('Elohim, then 'El). Zophar's speech ends where it is meant to lead: God is the one who brings the wicked to ruin.
'Adam is a human being, man or woman; Literal uses the gender setting.

The Hebrew singular means any wicked person (20:5, 29). Balanced and Readable use "they", which keeps the general sense; Literal follows the Hebrew "he" (as 8:14). Here Balanced and Readable say "the wicked" and "wicked people".
